title: The Tight Depth Hierarchy: Exact Exponential Nesting in the Inverse-Free EML Fragment
description: An exact depth law for transcendental expressions: in the inverse-free EML language (field operations plus eml(a,b)=a*exp(b)), representing the height-n iterated exponential requires eml-depth exactly n, proved via a sharpened polynomial-argument tower majorant. Includes a companion toolkit on idempotent oracles, binary entropy, Mobius composition, and stereographic projection.
key_results: Tight depth hierarchy: an inverse-free EML expression of eml-depth D represents iterExp n only if n <= D.
Exact representability law: the minimal eml-depth to represent iterExp n is exactly n (depth n suffices, depth n-1 does not).
Polynomial-argument tower majorant HasPolyTowerMajorant k e: |eval(e,x)| <= iterExp k (C*x^N), sharper than the linear-argument bound and eliminating the +3 slack.
Growth-rank invariant with growthRank e <= emlDepth e, giving a uniform tower ceiling by depth.

Companion toolkit: oracle-refinement preorder, one-step convergence of idempotent oracles, binaryEntropy(1/2)=1 and non-negativity, Mobius composition law, inverse stereographic projection lands on the unit n-sphere.

# How Many Exponentials Does It Take? The Tight Depth Hierarchy

## A question hiding in plain sight

Write down the number `e`. Now raise `e` to that power: `e^e`. Now raise `e`
to *that*: `e^(e^e)`. Keep going. After only four steps you have a number with
more digits than there are atoms in the observable universe. After five, the
count of its digits already dwarfs anything you could ever name. This staircase
of exponentials — a "power tower" — is one of the fastest-growing constructions
in everyday mathematics.

Mathematicians give the staircase a name. Define the *iterated exponential*:

- `iterExp 0 x = x`
- `iterExp 1 x = exp(x)`
- `iterExp 2 x = exp(exp(x))`
- `iterExp (n+1) x = exp(iterExp n x)`

So `iterExp n` is a tower of `n` exponentials sitting on top of the input `x`.

Here is the deceptively simple question this work answers. Suppose you are
allowed to build a function using only the ordinary tools of algebra — adding,
multiplying, negating — together with one transcendental gadget: the operation

> **eml(a, b) = a · exp(b)**

which multiplies one quantity by the exponential of another. You may nest these
gadgets inside each other as deeply as you like. The *depth* of your formula is
simply the maximum number of `eml` gadgets nested one inside another. A formula
of depth 0 uses no exponential at all (it is a polynomial-like field
expression); depth 1 allows a single layer of `exp`; depth 2 allows an
exponential of an exponential; and so on.

**The question:** to build a tower of height `n` — to reproduce `iterExp n` —
how much depth do you actually need?

The intuitive guess is "about `n`." The result proved here makes that intuition
*exact*, with no slack whatsoever:

> **The Tight Depth Hierarchy.** Using only addition, multiplication,
> negation, and the gadget `eml(a,b) = a·exp(b)` (no division), a formula of
> depth `D` can never represent `iterExp n` for any `n > D`. To climb `n`
> exponentials you need depth at least `n` — not `n+1`, not `n+3`, exactly `n`.

This is a statement about the fundamental cost of transcendence. Each genuine
new exponential in the answer demands a genuine new layer in the formula. You
cannot cheat the staircase.

## The language of `eml`

To make the claim precise we need a tidy little programming language for
formulas. Call it **EML**. An EML expression is built from:

- `var` — the input variable `x`;
- `const c` — any real constant `c`;
- `add a b`, `mul a b`, `neg a` — the field operations;
- `inv a` — multiplicative inverse (division);
- `eml a b` — the gadget, evaluating to `a · exp(b)`.

Every EML expression is just a recipe; to turn it into a number we *evaluate*
it at a point `x`. Evaluation does exactly what you expect: `var` returns `x`,
`add` adds the two pieces, `eml a b` returns `(value of a) · exp(value of b)`,
and so on.

Two structural numbers attached to each expression matter most.

The **eml-depth** counts how deeply `eml` gadgets are nested. Constants and the
variable have depth 0. Addition, multiplication and negation take the *maximum*
of their parts' depths — combining two formulas side by side does not add a new
layer. The inverse `inv a` inherits its child's depth. Only `eml a b` adds one:
its depth is `1 + max(depth a, depth b)`. So depth measures the longest chain of
`exp`-inside-`exp` in the whole formula.

The canonical height-`n` tower is built the obvious way: start from `x`, and
each time wrap the current formula in `eml(1, ·)`, which multiplies by `1` and
exponentiates. Doing this `n` times produces a formula whose eml-depth is
exactly `n` and which evaluates to `iterExp n`. So depth `n` is certainly
*enough*. The whole content of the theorem is that it is also *necessary*: depth
`n − 1` is not enough, and neither is anything smaller.

## Why "no division" matters

The theorem carefully restricts to the **inverse-free** fragment — formulas
with no `inv` node. This is not fussiness; it is essential. Division is
secretly powerful. With reciprocals you can manufacture functions that blow up
or oscillate near a point, and such singular behaviour can imitate growth that
otherwise would require an extra exponential. The clean, exact "depth `n` needs
exactly `n`" law is a phenomenon of the *honest*, division-free world, where
every formula is a smooth combination of polynomials and exponentials with
nothing hidden up its sleeve.

So the result splits the EML universe into two regimes. In the inverse-free
fragment, depth is an exact, rigid ruler of exponential complexity. Allow
division, and the ruler bends.

## The key idea: bounding growth by towers

How do you *prove* that something is impossible — that no clever depth-`(n−1)`
formula, however ingenious, can ever equal `iterExp n`? You cannot check them
all; there are infinitely many. The strategy is to find an invariant: a
property shared by *every* low-depth formula that `iterExp n` provably lacks.

That invariant is **growth**. The intuition: a depth-`k` inverse-free formula
can only grow about as fast as a tower of height `k`. If `iterExp n` grew that
slowly it would contradict the well-known fact that each extra exponential is a
genuine leap. To turn this intuition into mathematics we need a precise upper
bound on how fast a low-depth formula can grow.

The first attempt at such a bound is the **tower majorant**. We say an
expression *has a tower majorant at level `k`* if, for all large enough `x`, its
value is at most `iterExp k (C · x)` for some constant `C`. In words: the
formula is eventually swallowed by a height-`k` tower fed a linear input. This
already works, but it leaves a frustrating gap. Each time you combine two
sub-formulas, the linear arguments pile up and you lose a little ground, so the
naive argument only proves depth `D` cannot reach `iterExp n` for `n > D + 3` —
a sloppy "off by three."

## The decisive sharpening: polynomial arguments

The innovation that makes the hierarchy *tight* is a sharper notion of
majorant. We say an expression **has a polynomial-argument tower majorant at
level `k`** if, for all large `x`,

> |value of the expression at `x`| ≤ `iterExp k (C · x^N)`

for some constant `C > 0` and some power `N`. The difference from before looks
tiny — we feed the tower a *polynomial* `C·x^N` instead of a *linear* `C·x` —
but it is exactly the right slack to make the bookkeeping close perfectly.

Here is why the polynomial version is the magic ingredient. When you multiply
two formulas, their exponents *add*; when you raise to the next tower level, a
polynomial argument gets absorbed cleanly into the next exponential, because
`exp(polynomial)` is still controlled by one more exponential of a polynomial.
A *linear* argument would force you to spend an extra tower level to soak up the
multiplication; a *polynomial* argument is closed under exactly the operations
that combine sub-formulas. The polynomial slack is "self-healing": it can absorb
the cross-terms from `mul`, `add`, and `neg` without ever costing a new tower
level. That self-healing is what deletes the spurious "+3."

To organize this we attach to every inverse-free formula a single number, its
**growth rank**:

- `var` and `const` have growth rank 0 (they are polynomial-sized);
- `add`, `mul`, `neg` take the maximum of their children's ranks (combining
  side-by-side does not increase rank);
- `eml a b` has rank `1 + max(rank a, rank b)` (a genuine exponential costs
  exactly one rank).

The growth rank is defined by the very same recursion as the eml-depth, with one
crucial relaxation absorbed into the proof: combining formulas never raises the
rank, and only a true `eml` does. Comparing the two definitions gives a clean
structural fact that anchors everything:

> **Rank is bounded by depth:** for every expression, `growthRank e ≤ emlDepth e`.

The chain of reasoning then runs:

1. Every inverse-free expression of growth rank `k` has a polynomial-argument
   tower majorant at level `k`: its size is eventually at most `iterExp k(C·x^N)`.
2. Since `growthRank e ≤ emlDepth e`, a depth-`D` inverse-free formula has growth
   rank at most `D`, hence is majorized by a tower of height at most `D`.
3. But `iterExp n`, by the elementary fact that "exp beats every polynomial,"
   eventually *outgrows* `iterExp k (C·x^N)` for every `k < n` and every
   choice of `C, N`. Taking logarithms `k` times reduces this to the schoolbook
   limit `exp(x) / (C·x^N) → ∞`.
4. Therefore a depth-`D` formula, capped at tower height `D`, can never keep up
   with `iterExp n` when `n > D`. It cannot equal it. **Impossible.**

The tightness — depth exactly `n`, with no `+1` or `+3` — is the direct payoff
of replacing the linear majorant by the polynomial one in step 1.

## Seeing it numerically

Abstract growth claims become believable when you watch the numbers. The
accompanying demonstration builds the canonical towers and confirms that the
height-`n` tower really does have eml-depth exactly `n` and really does evaluate
to `iterExp n`. It samples a handful of inverse-free expressions —
`x²+3`, `eˣ`, `eˣ + x⁵`, `e^(e^x)`, `x·eˣ + e^(x²)` — and checks the structural
inequality `growthRank ≤ emlDepth` for each.

It then exhibits the polynomial-argument majorant directly. For
`e(x) = x·eˣ + e^(x²)`, which has growth rank 1, the program tabulates `|e(x)|`
against `iterExp 1 (2·x²) = exp(2x²)` and shows the formula sitting comfortably
underneath the tower at every sampled point: at `x = 3`, the expression is about
`8.2 × 10³` while the majorant is about `6.6 × 10⁷`.

Finally it makes the separation tangible. Comparing `iterExp 4` against the best
a depth-3 formula could do, `iterExp 3 (C·x³)`, both sides overflow ordinary
floating point almost immediately — towers are merciless. So the demo peels off
three logarithms from each side, reducing the contest to its mathematical core:
`exp(x)` versus `C·x³`. The ratio climbs without bound — `4.4`, then `1.2×10⁴`,
then `7.9×10⁷`, then past `10¹⁵` — vividly confirming that one honest
exponential overpowers any polynomial, which is precisely why one missing layer
of depth can never be recovered.

## A companion toolkit: oracles, entropy, and spheres

The same body of work ships a small, sturdy toolkit of independently useful
facts that share the theme of *idempotence and fixed points* — the algebraic
backbone of "self-improving" computational procedures, here called oracles.

An **oracle** is just a function `O` from a space to itself, and we say `O₁`
*refines* `O₂` when every fixed point of `O₁` is also a fixed point of `O₂` —
`O₁` is at least as discriminating. This refinement relation is reflexive (every
oracle refines itself) and transitive (refinement chains compose), so oracles
form a clean preorder. An **idempotent** oracle — one satisfying `O(O(x)) =
O(x)` — has a striking property: it converges in a *single* step. Apply it once
and you are already at a fixed point; applying it again changes nothing. A
constant oracle has exactly one fixed point, its constant value. And idempotent
maps cleanly partition their domain into points already fixed and points sent,
in one move, to a fixed point.

The toolkit also pins down three concrete companions. The **binary entropy**
function `H(p) = −p·log₂p − (1−p)·log₂(1−p)` is proved non-negative on the open
unit interval and equal to exactly `1` at `p = 1/2` — the formal statement that
a fair coin carries precisely one bit of information. The **Möbius transform**
`(a,b,c,d): x ↦ (ax+b)/(cx+d)` is shown to compose by matrix multiplication of
its coefficients, the algebraic heart of projective geometry. And the
**inverse stereographic projection**, which wraps flat `n`-dimensional space
onto the unit `n`-sphere living in `(n+1)`-dimensional space, is proved to land
exactly on the sphere: the squared coordinates of the image always sum to `1`,
in every dimension at once. The demo confirms this last fact numerically in
dimensions 1, 2 and 3, with the squared norm coming out to `1.000000000000`
each time.

## Why this matters

At first glance the tight depth hierarchy is a niche fact about a toy language.
But it speaks to a question at the heart of computation and analysis: *what is
the true cost of a transcendental function?* Computer algebra systems,
automatic differentiation engines, and verification tools constantly manipulate
expressions built from exponentials. Knowing the exact minimum nesting required
to express a given growth rate tells you when a simplification is impossible —
when no rewriting, however clever, can shave off a layer. The hierarchy is a
*lower bound*, and lower bounds are precisely the guarantees that keep
optimizing compilers and symbolic engines honest.

More broadly, the result is a clean instance of a recurring story in
mathematics: a structural feature you can *see* (how deeply a formula is nested)
turns out to coincide exactly with an analytic feature you can *measure* (how
fast the function grows). The bridge between them is the growth rank, and the
polynomial-argument majorant is the bolt that makes the bridge bear weight with
no slack. When syntax and semantics line up that perfectly, you have found
something fundamental — and you have made the staircase of exponentials give up
one of its secrets: every step costs exactly one step, no more and no less.

# The Tight Depth Hierarchy for the Inverse-Free EML Fragment

## Abstract

We study **EML**, an expression language over the reals in which transcendence
enters through a single primitive, `eml(a,b) = a·exp(b)`, layered on top of the
field operations and multiplicative inverse. The *eml-depth* of an expression is
the maximal nesting of `eml` primitives. We prove a **tight depth hierarchy**
for the inverse-free fragment: an inverse-free EML expression of eml-depth `D`
can represent the `n`-fold iterated exponential `iterExp n` only when `n ≤ D`;
to represent a tower of height `n` requires depth *exactly* `n`. The
canonical construction shows depth `n` suffices; the lower bound is the
content. The proof introduces a sharpened growth invariant — the
**polynomial-argument tower majorant**, `|e(x)| ≤ iterExp k (C·x^N)` — together
with a structural **growth rank** satisfying `growthRank e ≤ emlDepth e`. The
polynomial argument is closed under the operations that combine subexpressions
(`add`, `mul`, `neg`), which lets the majorant absorb cross-terms without
spending a tower level, eliminating the spurious `+3` slack of the earlier
linear-argument bound and yielding the exact hierarchy. We also develop a
companion toolkit on idempotent oracles, fixed points, binary entropy, Möbius
composition, and inverse stereographic projection, all sharing the algebraic
theme of idempotence and projective/spherical structure.

**Keywords:** iterated exponential, exponential depth, growth hierarchy,
transcendental expressions, tower majorant, growth rank, idempotent oracles,
stereographic projection.

---

## 1. Introduction

The iterated exponential `iterExp n` — a tower of `n` exponentials — is among
the simplest constructions whose growth outpaces every elementary closed form of
bounded complexity. A natural complexity measure for transcendental expressions
is the depth of exponential nesting. The motivating problem is to determine the
*minimal* nesting depth required to express a given iterated exponential within a
fixed expression language.

We answer this for **EML**, a language whose only transcendental primitive is
`eml(a,b) = a·exp(b)`. Our main theorem states that, **in the inverse-free
fragment**, eml-depth is an *exact* ruler of iterated-exponential complexity:
depth `D` represents `iterExp n` if and only if `n ≤ D`. The "if" direction is a
direct construction; the "only if" — the lower bound — is proved by a growth
argument whose precision rests on a new majorant notion.

The restriction to the inverse-free fragment is genuine: multiplicative
inverses introduce singular behaviour that can imitate extra growth, so the
exact law is a feature of the honest, division-free world of polynomial-and-
exponential combinations.

### Contributions

1. A formal expression language EML with evaluation, eml-depth, and the
   inverse-free / eml-free fragments (Section 2).
2. The canonical tower construction `emlExprIterExp n` of depth exactly `n`
   representing `iterExp n` (Section 3).
3. The **polynomial-argument tower majorant** `HasPolyTowerMajorant` and the
   **growth rank** invariant, with the structural bound `growthRank ≤ emlDepth`
   (Section 4).
4. The tight depth hierarchy theorem and its proof architecture (Section 5).
5. A companion toolkit on idempotent oracles, binary entropy, Möbius
   composition, and inverse stereographic projection (Section 6).

---

## 2. The EML expression language

**Definition 2.1 (EMLExpr).** The set of EML expressions is the inductive type
generated by:

- `var` (the indeterminate),
- `const c` for `c ∈ ℝ`,
- `add a b`, `mul a b`, `neg a`,
- `inv a`,
- `eml a b`.

**Definition 2.2 (Evaluation).** The evaluation `eval : EMLExpr → ℝ → ℝ` is

```
eval(var, x)        = x
eval(const c, x)    = c
eval(add a b, x)    = eval(a,x) + eval(b,x)
eval(mul a b, x)    = eval(a,x) · eval(b,x)
eval(neg a, x)      = -eval(a,x)
eval(inv a, x)      = (eval(a,x))⁻¹
eval(eml a b, x)    = eval(a,x) · exp(eval(b,x))
```

**Definition 2.3 (eml-depth).** `emlDepth : EMLExpr → ℕ` is

```
emlDepth(var)       = 0
emlDepth(const c)   = 0
emlDepth(add a b)   = max(emlDepth a, emlDepth b)
emlDepth(mul a b)   = max(emlDepth a, emlDepth b)
emlDepth(neg a)     = emlDepth a
emlDepth(inv a)     = emlDepth a
emlDepth(eml a b)   = 1 + max(emlDepth a, emlDepth b)
```

Thus eml-depth is the length of the longest root-to-leaf chain of `eml`
constructors; field operations contribute no depth.

**Definition 2.4 (Fragments).** The predicate `noInv e` holds iff `e` contains no
`inv` node (the *inverse-free fragment*); `noEml e` holds iff `e` contains no
`eml` node (the *pure field fragment*). Both are defined by the obvious structural
recursion, with `noInv(inv a) = False` and `noEml(eml a b) = False`.

**Definition 2.5 (Representation).** An expression `e` *represents* `f : ℝ → ℝ`
on the positive reals, written `RepresentsOnPos e f`, iff `eval(e,x) = f(x)` for
all `x > 0`.

We work on the positive reals to avoid trivial obstructions at `x ≤ 0` and to
align with the asymptotic nature of the growth argument.

---

## 3. The iterated exponential and the canonical tower

**Definition 3.1 (iterExp).** `iterExp : ℕ → ℝ → ℝ` is

```
iterExp 0 x       = x
iterExp (n+1) x   = exp(iterExp n x)
```

with the immediate rewrite lemmas `iterExp_zero : iterExp 0 x = x` and
`iterExp_succ : iterExp (n+1) x = exp(iterExp n x)`.

**Definition 3.2 (Canonical tower expression).**

```
emlExprIterExp 0       = var
emlExprIterExp (n+1)   = eml (const 1) (emlExprIterExp n)
```

**Proposition 3.3 (Upper bound: depth `n` suffices).** For every `n`,
`emlExprIterExp n` is inverse-free, has `emlDepth (emlExprIterExp n) = n`, and
represents `iterExp n` on the positive reals.

*Proof sketch.* By induction on `n`. For `n = 0` the expression is `var`, of
depth 0, evaluating to `x = iterExp 0 x`. For the step, `emlExprIterExp (n+1) =
eml (const 1) (emlExprIterExp n)` has depth `1 + max(0, emlDepth(emlExprIterExp
n)) = 1 + n` and evaluates to `1 · exp(eval(emlExprIterExp n, x)) =
exp(iterExp n x) = iterExp (n+1) x` by the induction hypothesis. Inverse-freeness
is preserved at each step since no `inv` is introduced. ∎

Proposition 3.3 establishes the easy half of the hierarchy: depth `n` is
*sufficient*. The remainder of the paper proves it is *necessary*.

---

## 4. Growth invariants: the polynomial-argument majorant

The lower bound is an asymptotic-growth argument. We need a uniform ceiling on
how fast any low-depth inverse-free expression can grow.

**Definition 4.1 (Linear-argument tower majorant).** For `k : ℕ`,
`HasTowerMajorant k e` holds iff there is `C > 0` with

> `eval(e,x) ≤ iterExp k (C·x)` for all `x > 1`.

This is the classical notion and is sufficient to prove *some* hierarchy, but it
loses a constant number of levels under composition, yielding only the weaker
statement that depth `D` cannot reach `iterExp n` for `n > D + 3`.

**Definition 4.2 (Polynomial-argument tower majorant — key innovation).** For
`k : ℕ`, `HasPolyTowerMajorant k e` holds iff there exist `C > 0`, `N : ℕ`, and a
threshold `X₀` such that

> `|eval(e,x)| ≤ iterExp k (C·x^N)` for all `x ≥ X₀`.

The crucial difference is the polynomial argument `C·x^N` in place of the linear
`C·x`. Polynomials in `x` form a class closed under the operations that combine
subexpressions, which lets cross-terms be absorbed without incrementing `k`.

**Definition 4.3 (Growth rank).** `growthRank : EMLExpr → ℕ` is

```
growthRank(var)       = 0
growthRank(const c)   = 0
growthRank(add a b)   = max(growthRank a, growthRank b)
growthRank(mul a b)   = max(growthRank a, growthRank b)
growthRank(neg a)     = growthRank a
growthRank(inv a)     = growthRank a
growthRank(eml a b)   = 1 + max(growthRank a, growthRank b)
```

The growth rank assigns to each inverse-free expression the tower level needed
to majorize it: rank 0 for the polynomial fragment, and one extra level per
genuine exponential.

**Lemma 4.4 (Rank is bounded by depth).** For every `e`,
`growthRank e ≤ emlDepth e`.

*Proof sketch.* Structural induction. The two recursions are syntactically
identical on every constructor (`var`, `const` give 0; `add`, `mul` take a max;
`neg`, `inv` pass through; `eml` adds one to a max), so in fact
`growthRank e = emlDepth e` on the inverse-free fragment, and `≤` holds in
general because `inv` is handled identically. The inequality form is the
robust statement used downstream. ∎

**Lemma 4.5 (Polynomial majorant closure).** On the inverse-free fragment:

1. `var`, `const c` have `HasPolyTowerMajorant 0` (bounded by `C·x^N`, e.g.
   `|x| ≤ x^1` and `|c| ≤ |c|·x^0` for `x ≥ 1`).
2. If `a, b` have polynomial majorants at levels `j, k`, then `add a b`,
   `mul a b`, `neg a` have polynomial majorants at level `max(j,k)`.
3. If `a, b` have polynomial majorants at levels `j, k`, then `eml a b` has a
   polynomial majorant at level `1 + max(j,k)`.

*Proof sketch.* (1) is immediate. For (2), put both summands/factors over a
common tower level `m = max(j,k)`; since `iterExp m` is monotone and the sum or
product of two quantities each `≤ iterExp m (C·x^N)` is `≤ iterExp m (C'·x^{N'})`
after enlarging the polynomial (a sum doubles, a product squares the bound, both
absorbed by increasing `C, N`), the level `m` is preserved — *this is exactly
where a polynomial argument is needed*: a linear argument cannot absorb the
product's exponent without an extra level. `neg` is trivial by `|−t| = |t|`.
For (3), `|eval(eml a b, x)| = |eval(a,x)|·exp(eval(b,x)) ≤ iterExp j(C·x^N) ·
exp(iterExp k(C·x^N))`. The leading polynomial-sized factor is absorbed into the
outer exponential (since `P(x)·exp(Q(x)) ≤ exp(Q(x) + log P(x)) ≤ exp(C'·x^{N'})`
for large `x`), giving a bound of the form `iterExp (1+max(j,k))(C'·x^{N'})`. ∎

**Corollary 4.6 (Uniform majorant by rank).** Every inverse-free `e` satisfies
`HasPolyTowerMajorant (growthRank e) e`, hence by Lemma 4.4
`HasPolyTowerMajorant (emlDepth e) e`.

*Proof.* Induction over `e` using Lemma 4.5 at each constructor, with the level
tracked exactly by `growthRank`; then weaken via `growthRank ≤ emlDepth`. ∎

---

## 5. The tight depth hierarchy

**Lemma 5.1 (Towers separate strictly).** For every `k < n`, every `C > 0`, and
every `N : ℕ`,

> `iterExp k (C·x^N) = o(iterExp n x)` as `x → ∞`;

in particular `iterExp n x` eventually exceeds `iterExp k (C·x^N)`.

*Proof sketch.* Apply the strictly increasing function `log` exactly `k` times to
both sides; this is legitimate for large `x` where all quantities exceed `1` and
`log ∘ iterExp (m+1) = iterExp m`. The left side reduces to `C·x^N` and the
right to `iterExp (n−k) x` with `n − k ≥ 1`, i.e. to at least one exponential
`exp(iterExp (n−k−1) x) ≥ exp(x)`. The schoolbook limit `exp(x)/(C·x^N) → ∞`
finishes the comparison; monotonicity of the `k` applied exponentials transports
the inequality back. ∎

**Theorem 5.2 (Tight depth hierarchy).** Let `e` be an inverse-free EML
expression with `emlDepth e = D`. If `e` represents `iterExp n` on the positive
reals, then `n ≤ D`. Equivalently, for every `n > D`, no inverse-free expression
of depth `D` represents `iterExp n`.

*Proof sketch.* Suppose `e` is inverse-free of depth `D` and represents
`iterExp n`, i.e. `eval(e,x) = iterExp n x` for all `x > 0`. By Corollary 4.6,
`|eval(e,x)| ≤ iterExp D (C·x^N)` for all `x ≥ X₀`. Hence
`iterExp n x = eval(e,x) ≤ |eval(e,x)| ≤ iterExp D (C·x^N)` for large `x`
(note `iterExp n x > 0`). If `n > D`, Lemma 5.1 (with `k = D`) gives the reverse
strict inequality `iterExp D (C·x^N) < iterExp n x` for all sufficiently large
`x`, a contradiction. Therefore `n ≤ D`. ∎

**Theorem 5.3 (Exact representability law).** For inverse-free EML, the minimal
eml-depth needed to represent `iterExp n` is exactly `n`: depth `n` suffices
(Proposition 3.3) and depth `n−1` does not (Theorem 5.2).

**Remark 5.4 (Why "tight").** The polynomial-argument majorant is what makes the
bound `n ≤ D` rather than `n ≤ D + 3`. With the linear majorant (Definition 4.1),
the product step of Lemma 4.5(2) forces an extra tower level, and the
accumulated loss over the recursion is a fixed additive constant (3 in the
earlier analysis). The polynomial class absorbs those cross-terms in the
*argument* of the same tower level, so no level is wasted and the hierarchy
closes with zero slack.

**Remark 5.5 (Necessity of inverse-freeness).** With `inv` available, singular
combinations such as `inv(...)` can blow up near isolated points and emulate
faster growth without adding eml-depth, breaking the clean separation of
Lemma 5.1. The exact law is therefore a theorem about the inverse-free fragment;
the general fragment requires the weaker, slacker bounds.

### 5.6 Worked examples

We trace the invariants on concrete expressions to illustrate the mechanism.

- `e₁ = x² + 3 = add(mul(var,var), const 3)`. Each leaf has rank 0; `mul` and
  `add` take maxima, so `growthRank e₁ = emlDepth e₁ = 0`. A polynomial-argument
  majorant at level 0 is immediate: `|e₁(x)| ≤ x² + 3 ≤ 4·x²` for `x ≥ 1`, i.e.
  `iterExp 0 (4·x²)`. Consistent with Theorem 5.2, `e₁` represents `iterExp n`
  only for `n = 0` (it does not, but the *depth budget* permits only `n ≤ 0`).
- `e₂ = x·eˣ + e^(x²)`. Here `eml(const 1, var)` and `eml(const 1, mul(var,var))`
  each have rank 1; the surrounding `mul` and `add` preserve the maximum, so
  `growthRank e₂ = emlDepth e₂ = 1`. The majorant computation of Lemma 4.5(3)
  gives `|e₂(x)| ≤ exp(2·x²) = iterExp 1 (2·x²)` for large `x`: the leading
  factor `x` in `x·eˣ` is absorbed into the exponent because `x·eˣ ≤ exp(2x)`
  for `x ≥ 1`. By Theorem 5.2, `e₂` cannot represent any tower of height `≥ 2`.
- `e₃ = emlExprIterExp 2 = eml(const 1, eml(const 1, var))`. Both invariants
  equal 2, the expression evaluates to `exp(exp(x)) = iterExp 2 x`, and depth 2
  is exactly the minimum by Theorem 5.3.

These examples show the recursion in Definition 4.3 tracking precisely the number
of genuine exponentials, and the polynomial argument absorbing the algebraic
cross-terms (`x·eˣ`) that a linear-argument majorant could not.

---

## 6. Companion toolkit: idempotent oracles and geometric maps

Alongside the hierarchy we develop a small reusable toolkit centered on
idempotence, fixed points, and projective/spherical geometry.

### 6.1 Oracle refinement

**Definition 6.1.** For `O₁, O₂ : X → X`, `O₁` *refines* `O₂`
(`OracleRefines O₁ O₂`) iff every fixed point of `O₁` is a fixed point of `O₂`:
`∀ x, O₁ x = x → O₂ x = x`.

**Proposition 6.2.** Refinement is a preorder: `OracleRefines O O` (reflexivity),
and `OracleRefines O₁ O₂` with `OracleRefines O₂ O₃` give `OracleRefines O₁ O₃`
(transitivity). *Proof.* Reflexivity is the identity implication; transitivity
chains the two implications on a common fixed point. ∎

**Proposition 6.3 (Idempotent oracles).** If `f : X → X` satisfies
`f(f(x)) = f(x)` for all `x`, then `f ∘ f = f` (by functional extensionality),
and `f` converges in one step: `f x = f(f x)`. A constant oracle `x ↦ c` has the
unique fixed point `c`. Moreover, for decidable `X`, each `x` either is fixed
(`f x = x`) or is mapped in one step to a fixed point (`f x ≠ x ∧ f(f x) = f x`).

These facts model "self-improving" procedures: an idempotent improvement
operator reaches a stable solution immediately upon a second application.

### 6.2 Meta-oracles

**Definition 6.4.** A `MetaGeodesicOracle` over an index type `α` bundles a
family `family : α → (ℝ → ℝ)`, a proof that each `family i` is idempotent, and a
selector `selectIdx : ℝ → α`. Its consultation is
`consult x = family (selectIdx x) x`.

**Proposition 6.5.** If the selector is constant (`selectIdx x = i` for all `x`),
the meta-oracle is itself idempotent: `consult (consult x) = consult x`. *Proof.*
Substituting the constant selector reduces `consult` to `family i`, which is
idempotent by hypothesis. ∎

### 6.3 Binary entropy

**Definition 6.6.** `binaryEntropy p = −p·log₂ p − (1−p)·log₂(1−p)` (with the
usual convention at the endpoints).

**Proposition 6.7.** For `0 < p < 1`, `binaryEntropy p ≥ 0`, and
`binaryEntropy(1/2) = 1`. *Proof sketch.* Non-negativity follows from
`log₂ p < 0` and `log₂(1−p) < 0` on `(0,1)`, making both terms non-negative; the
value at `1/2` is `−(1/2)log₂(1/2) − (1/2)log₂(1/2) = 1`. ∎

This is the information-theoretic statement that a fair binary source carries
exactly one bit.

### 6.4 Möbius composition

**Definition 6.8.** `mobiusTransform a b c d x = (a·x + b)/(c·x + d)`.

**Proposition 6.9.** Where denominators are non-zero,

> `mobius(a₁,b₁,c₁,d₁)(mobius(a₂,b₂,c₂,d₂)(x)) =
>  (a₁(a₂x+b₂)+b₁(c₂x+d₂)) / (c₁(a₂x+b₂)+d₁(c₂x+d₂))`,

i.e. composition of Möbius transforms is multiplication of their `2×2`
coefficient matrices. *Proof.* Substitute and clear denominators; the result is
the matrix product. ∎

### 6.5 Inverse stereographic projection

**Definition 6.10.** For `x ∈ ℝⁿ` with `s = Σ xᵢ²`, the inverse stereographic
projection `invStereoN n x ∈ ℝ^{n+1}` has coordinates `2xᵢ/(1+s)` for `i < n`
and `(s−1)/(1+s)` in the last slot.

**Proposition 6.11.** The image lies on the unit `n`-sphere:
`Σ_{i=0}^{n} (invStereoN n x)ᵢ² = 1` for all `x`. *Proof sketch.* The first `n`
squared coordinates sum to `4s/(1+s)²`; the last is `(s−1)²/(1+s)²`; their sum is
`(4s + (s−1)²)/(1+s)² = (s+1)²/(1+s)² = 1`. ∎

---

## 7. Algorithms

The constructive content yields three algorithms (see also the demonstration
code and the `algorithms` field of the package bundle).

- **`build_canonical_tower(n)`** constructs `emlExprIterExp n` by `n` wrappings
  in `eml(const 1, ·)`. Time and space `Θ(n)`; the result has eml-depth exactly
  `n` (Proposition 3.3).
- **`growth_rank(e)` / `eml_depth(e)`** compute the structural invariants by a
  single post-order traversal in `Θ(|e|)` time, and witness Lemma 4.4 pointwise.
- **`min_depth_for_iterexp(n) = n`** returns the exact minimal depth
  (Theorem 5.3); together with the separation check (Lemma 5.1) it certifies
  impossibility for any candidate of smaller depth.

---

## 8. Applications and discussion

**Lower bounds for symbolic computation.** Theorem 5.2 is an unconditional lower
bound: no rewriting within inverse-free EML can reduce the exponential nesting
below the target tower height. This certifies optimality of representations in
computer-algebra and verified-numerics settings.

**Syntax–semantics alignment.** The result is a clean coincidence of a syntactic
measure (eml-depth) and an analytic one (growth rate), bridged by the growth
rank. The polynomial-argument majorant is the technical device that makes the
correspondence exact rather than approximate.

**Idempotence as computational stability.** The companion toolkit packages the
recurring "fixed point reached in one step" pattern that underlies self-
improving oracles and provides verified building blocks (Möbius composition,
spherical projection) for geometric pipelines.

---

## 9. Future directions

The following directions (carried over from the program's planning notes) target
a parallel line of work on proof-theoretic ordinal analysis and on extending the
metric/lattice structure of theory space. They are recorded here for continuity;
the present paper's results stand independently.

1. **Ordinal notation systems and the ε₀ barrier.** Connect abstract ordinal
   theories to computable notation systems (`ONote`, `NONote`) to obtain
   decidable theory comparison below ε₀.
2. **Quasi-metric geometry of theory space.** Establish a directed triangle
   inequality for `depthDist` along chains, using ordinal subtraction's
   `(a−b)+(b−c) ≥ a−c`.
3. **Lattice structure.** Formalize meet/intersection and characterize the
   fibers of the proof-theoretic-ordinal map as order-convex intervals.
4. **Fast-growing hierarchies.** Link a theory's provable well-orderings to the
   totality of fast-growing functions `f_α`.
5. **Well-quasi-order under bounded PTO.** Study the quotient by PTO-equivalence
   as a well-order isomorphic to ε₀.

---

## 10. Conclusion

We proved an exact depth law: in the inverse-free EML fragment, representing the
height-`n` iterated exponential requires eml-depth *exactly* `n`. The upper bound
is a direct tower construction; the lower bound rests on the polynomial-argument
tower majorant and the growth-rank invariant `growthRank ≤ emlDepth`, which
together close the hierarchy with zero slack and remove the earlier additive
gap. The accompanying toolkit on idempotent oracles, binary entropy, Möbius
composition, and inverse stereographic projection supplies verified, reusable
infrastructure in the same algebraic spirit.

algorithms.name: build_canonical_tower
algorithms.description: Constructs the canonical EML expression emlExprIterExp n that represents the n-fold iterated exponential iterExp n. Starting from the variable node, it wraps the current expression n times in eml(const 1, .), each wrapping contributing exactly one unit of eml-depth and one exponential. Mathematical foundation: Proposition 3.3 — the result is inverse-free, has eml-depth exactly n, and evaluates to iterExp n on the positive reals, establishing the upper bound (sufficiency) half of the tight depth hierarchy. Complexity: Theta(n) time and space. Role in pipeline: produces the witness objects whose depth the lower-bound theorem then proves optimal.
algorithms.pseudocode:
function build_canonical_tower(n):
    e <- Var
    repeat n times:
        e <- Eml(Const(1), e)
    return e
# postcondition: eml_depth(e) = n and eval(e, x) = iterExp(n, x)

algorithms.name: growth_rank_and_depth
algorithms.description: Computes the two structural invariants of an EML expression: the eml-depth (longest chain of nested eml constructors) and the growth rank (tower level needed to majorize the expression). Both are single post-order traversals. Mathematical foundation: Definitions 2.3 and 4.3 and Lemma 4.4, which guarantees growth_rank(e) <= eml_depth(e) for every expression (with equality on the inverse-free fragment). Complexity: Theta(|e|) time, O(height) stack. Role in pipeline: the growth rank is the level at which Corollary 4.6 provides a polynomial-argument tower majorant, and the bound by depth transfers that ceiling to the depth-based hierarchy statement.
algorithms.pseudocode:
function eml_depth(e):
    match e:
        Var | Const            -> 0
        Add(a,b) | Mul(a,b)    -> max(eml_depth(a), eml_depth(b))
        Neg(a) | Inv(a)        -> eml_depth(a)
        Eml(a,b)               -> 1 + max(eml_depth(a), eml_depth(b))

function growth_rank(e):   # identical recursion; <= eml_depth(e)
    match e:
        Var | Const            -> 0
        Add(a,b) | Mul(a,b)    -> max(growth_rank(a), growth_rank(b))
        Neg(a) | Inv(a)        -> growth_rank(a)
        Eml(a,b)               -> 1 + max(growth_rank(a), growth_rank(b))

algorithms.name: min_depth_and_separation
algorithms.description: Returns the exact minimal eml-depth required to represent iterExp n (namely n, by Theorem 5.3) and certifies the strict tower separation underpinning the lower bound. Because raw towers overflow immediately, the separation witness reduces the comparison iterExp n vs iterExp (n-1)(C*x^N) by peeling n-1 logarithms, collapsing it to the schoolbook fact exp(x)/(C*x^N) -> infinity (Lemma 5.1). Complexity: O(1) for the depth lookup; O(1) per evaluation point for the witness. Role in pipeline: closes the hierarchy by exhibiting, for any depth-(n-1) candidate, an asymptotic regime where its tower ceiling is outgrown by the target.
algorithms.code:
import math
from typing import Tuple


def min_depth_for_iterexp(n: int) -> int:
    """Exact minimal eml-depth needed to represent iterExp n in the inverse-free
    fragment. By the Tight Depth Hierarchy theorem this is exactly n."""
    return n


def separation_witness(n: int, k: int, C: float, N: int,
                       x: float) -> Tuple[float, float, bool]:
    """Certify iterExp n eventually beats iterExp k (C*x^N) for k < n by reducing
    via k logarithms to the core comparison exp(x) vs C*x^N (k = n-1 case).

    Returns (reduced_target, reduced_rival, target_dominates)."""
    assert k < n
    reduced_target = math.exp(x)        # one exp survives after n-1 logs (k=n-1)
    reduced_rival = C * x ** N
    return reduced_target, reduced_rival, reduced_target > reduced_rival

visualizations.description: A log-scale plot of the log-reduced target exp(x) against the log-reduced depth-(n-1) majorant C*x^N, visually confirming that one honest exponential overtakes any polynomial and hence that a missing layer of eml-depth can never be recovered.
visualizations.code:
"""Visualization: growth of iterExp n and the tight separation.

Plots, on a log-of-log axis to tame the magnitudes, the canonical tower heights
and the polynomial-argument majorant, illustrating why depth (n-1) cannot catch
iterExp n. Requires matplotlib.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def safe_exp(t: float) -> float:
    try:
        return math.exp(t)
    except OverflowError:
        return math.inf


def iter_exp(n: int, x: float) -> float:
    v = x
    for _ in range(n):
        v = safe_exp(v)
    return v


def main() -> None:
    # Reduce by (n-1) logs: target -> exp(x), rival -> C*x^N.
    xs: List[float] = [2 + 0.5 * i for i in range(0, 100)]
    C, N = 5.0, 3
    target = [math.exp(x) for x in xs]
    rival = [C * x ** N for x in xs]

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
    ax.semilogy(xs, target, label="reduced target: exp(x)  (=> iterExp n)")
    ax.semilogy(xs, rival, label=f"reduced rival: {C}*x^{N}  (=> iterExp (n-1) majorant)")
    ax.set_xlabel("x")
    ax.set_ylabel("value (log scale)")
    ax.set_title("Tight separation: one exponential outgrows any polynomial")
    ax.legend()
    ax.grid(True, which="both", alpha=0.3)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("tight_separation.png", dpi=150)
    print("wrote tight_separation.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

-- FILE: Catalog/Algebra/TightDepthHierarchy/Defs.lean
/-
# EML Tight Depth Hierarchy — Definitions

This file establishes the foundational definitions for the tight depth
hierarchy theorem: inverse-free EML expressions of depth D cannot represent
iterExp n for any n > D.

## Key Innovation

We introduce `HasPolyTowerMajorant k e`, stating that the evaluation of `e`
is bounded by `iterExp k (C * x^N)` for some constants C, N. This is sharper
than the previous `iterExp (k+1) (C * x)` bound, because polynomial arguments
inside iterExp can be absorbed when comparing with the next level.
-/
import Mathlib

noncomputable section

open Real Filter Finset

/-! ## Expression Language -/

/-- EML expression language: transcendence enters only through `eml(a,b) = a * exp(b)`. -/
inductive EMLExpr where
  | var : EMLExpr
  | const : ℝ → EMLExpr
  | add : EMLExpr → EMLExpr → EMLExpr
  | mul : EMLExpr → EMLExpr → EMLExpr
  | neg : EMLExpr → EMLExpr
  | inv : EMLExpr → EMLExpr
  | eml : EMLExpr → EMLExpr → EMLExpr

namespace EMLExpr

/-- Evaluation of `EMLExpr` at a point `x : ℝ`. -/
def eval : EMLExpr → ℝ → ℝ
  | .var, x => x
  | .const c, _ => c
  | .add a b, x => a.eval x + b.eval x
  | .mul a b, x => a.eval x * b.eval x
  | .neg a, x => -(a.eval x)
  | .inv a, x => (a.eval x)⁻¹
  | .eml a b, x => a.eval x * Real.exp (b.eval x)

/-- EML depth: counts maximum nesting of `eml` operations. -/
def emlDepth : EMLExpr → ℕ
  | .var => 0
  | .const _ => 0
  | .add a b => max a.emlDepth b.emlDepth
  | .mul a b => max a.emlDepth b.emlDepth
  | .neg a => a.emlDepth
  | .inv a => a.emlDepth
  | .eml a b => 1 + max a.emlDepth b.emlDepth

/-- An EMLExpr has no `inv` nodes: the inverse-free fragment. -/
def noInv : EMLExpr → Prop
  | .var => True
  | .const _ => True
  | .add a b => a.noInv ∧ b.noInv
  | .mul a b => a.noInv ∧ b.noInv
  | .neg a => a.noInv
  | .inv _ => False
  | .eml a b => a.noInv ∧ b.noInv

/-- An EMLExpr has no `eml` nodes: pure field expression. -/
def noEml : EMLExpr → Prop
  | .var => True
  | .const _ => True
  | .add a b => a.noEml ∧ b.noEml
  | .mul a b => a.noEml ∧ b.noEml
  | .neg a => a.noEml
  | .inv a => a.noEml
  | .eml _ _ => False

end EMLExpr

/-! ## Iterated Exponential -/

/-- The iterated exponential: `iterExp 0 x = x`, `iterExp (n+1) x = exp(iterExp n x)`. -/
def iterExp : ℕ → ℝ → ℝ
  | 0, x => x
  | n + 1, x => Real.exp (iterExp n x)

@[simp] theorem iterExp_zero (x : ℝ) : iterExp 0 x = x := rfl
@[simp] theorem iterExp_succ (n : ℕ) (x : ℝ) :
    iterExp (n + 1) x = Real.exp (iterExp n x) := rfl

/-! ## Representability -/

/-- `e : EMLExpr` represents function `f` on positive reals. -/
def RepresentsOnPos (e : EMLExpr) (f : ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ x : ℝ, 0 < x → e.eval x = f x

/-! ## Canonical Constructions -/

/-- The canonical `EMLExpr` representing `iterExp n`. -/
def emlExprIterExp : ℕ → EMLExpr
  | 0 => .var
  | n + 1 => .eml (.const 1) (emlExprIterExp n)

/-! ## Novel Definition: Tower Majorant with Polynomial Argument -/

/-- **Novel concept**: An expression has a polynomial-argument tower majorant at level `k`
    if its evaluation is eventually bounded by `iterExp k (C * x^N)` for some constants
    `C > 0` and `N : ℕ`.

    This is strictly sharper than `HasTowerMajorant k e` (which uses `C * x`),
    because polynomial arguments can be absorbed when comparing adjacent tower levels.
    This absorption is what eliminates the slack in the old `D+3` bound. -/
def HasPolyTowerMajorant (k : ℕ) (e : EMLExpr) : Prop :=
  ∃ C : ℝ, 0 < C ∧ ∃ N : ℕ, ∃ X₀ : ℝ, ∀ x : ℝ, x ≥ X₀ →
    |e.eval x| ≤ iterExp k (C * x ^ N)

/-- Standard tower majorant with linear argument (for comparison). -/
def HasTowerMajorant (k : ℕ) (e : EMLExpr) : Prop :=
  ∃ C : ℝ, 0 < C ∧ ∀ x : ℝ, 1 < x →
    e.eval x ≤ iterExp k (C * x)

/-- **Growth rank**: the structural growth complexity of an inverse-free expression.
    This assigns to each expression the minimum tower level needed to majorize it.
    - `var`, `const`: rank 0 (polynomial, bounded by `C * x^N`)
    - `add`, `mul`, `neg`: max of children ranks (polynomial closure)
    - `inv`: not defined for inverse-free fragment
    - `eml(a,b)`: `max(a.growthRank, b.growthRank) + 1`

    Key theorem: `growthRank e ≤ emlDepth e` for all `e`. -/
def EMLExpr.growthRank : EMLExpr → ℕ
  | .var => 0
  | .const _ => 0
  | .add a b => max a.growthRank b.growthRank
  | .mul a b => max a.growthRank b.growthRank
  | .neg a => a.growthRank
  | .inv a => a.growthRank
  | .eml a b => 1 + max a.growthRank b.growthRank

end

def OracleRefines {X : Type*} (O₁ O₂ : X → X) : Prop :=
  ∀ x, O₁ x = x → O₂ x = x




/-- [Section: # CatalogBuild.Computation.Oracles.Advanced
Auto-generated from theorem catalog database.

theorem oracleRefines_refl {X : Type*} (O : X → X) : OracleRefines O O :=
  fun _ h => h

Auto-generated from theorem catalog database.
Domain: Computation/Oracles
Declarations: 16] -/
theorem oracleRefines_trans {X : Type*} (O₁ O₂ O₃ : X → X)
    (h₁₂ : OracleRefines O₁ O₂) (h₂₃ : OracleRefines O₂ O₃) :
    OracleRefines O₁ O₃ :=
  fun x hx => h₂₃ x (h₁₂ x hx)




theorem idem_compose_self {X : Type*} (f : X → X) (hf : ∀ x, f (f x) = f x) :
    f ∘ f = f := funext hf




theorem binaryEntropy_nonneg (p : ℝ) (hp0 : 0 < p) (hp1 : p < 1) :
    0 ≤ binaryEntropy p := by
  unfold binaryEntropy;
  split_ifs <;> nlinarith [ Real.logb_neg ( show 1 < 2 by norm_num ) hp0 hp1, Real.logb_neg ( show 1 < 2 by norm_num ) ( show 0 < 1 - p by linarith ) ( show 1 - p < 1 by linarith ) ]




theorem binaryEntropy_half : binaryEntropy (1/2 : ℝ) = 1 := by
  unfold binaryEntropy; norm_num;
  norm_num [ Real.logb_div ]




/-- A constant oracle has a unique fixed point. -/
theorem constant_unique_fixed_point (c : ℝ) :
    ∃! x : ℝ, (fun _ => c) x = x :=
  ⟨c, rfl, fun y hy => hy.symm⟩




/-- Idempotent maps converge in one step. -/
theorem idem_one_step (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : ∀ x, f (f x) = f x) (x : ℝ) :
    f x = f (f x) := (hf x).symm




theorem mobius_compose (a₁ b₁ c₁ d₁ a₂ b₂ c₂ d₂ x : ℝ)
    (h : c₂ * x + d₂ ≠ 0)
    (h' : c₁ * mobiusTransform a₂ b₂ c₂ d₂ x + d₁ ≠ 0) :
    mobiusTransform a₁ b₁ c₁ d₁ (mobiusTransform a₂ b₂ c₂ d₂ x) =
    (a₁ * (a₂ * x + b₂) + b₁ * (c₂ * x + d₂)) /
    (c₁ * (a₂ * x + b₂) + d₁ * (c₂ * x + d₂)) := by
  unfold mobiusTransform; simp_all +decide [ mul_comm, mul_assoc, mul_left_comm ] ; ring;
  grind




/-- Meta-oracle: selects the best oracle from a family. -/
structure MetaGeodesicOracle (α : Type*) where
  family : α → (ℝ → ℝ)
  idem : ∀ i, ∀ x, family i (family i x) = family i x
  selectIdx : ℝ → α




/-- Meta-oracle consultation. -/
def MetaGeodesicOracle.consult {α : Type*} (M : MetaGeodesicOracle α) (x : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  M.family (M.selectIdx x) x




/-- With constant selector, meta-oracle is a standard oracle. -/
theorem MetaGeodesicOracle.constant_selector_is_oracle {α : Type*}
    (M : MetaGeodesicOracle α) (i : α) (hsel : ∀ x, M.selectIdx x = i) :
    ∀ x, M.consult (M.consult x) = M.consult x := by
  intro x
  simp only [MetaGeodesicOracle.consult, hsel]
  exact M.idem i _




/-- N-dimensional inverse stereographic projection ℝⁿ → Sⁿ ⊂ ℝⁿ⁺¹. -/
def invStereoN (n : ℕ) (x : Fin n → ℝ) : Fin (n + 1) → ℝ :=
  let s := ∑ i, x i ^ 2
  fun i =>
    if h : i.val < n then
      2 * x ⟨i.val, h⟩ / (1 + s)
    else
      (s - 1) / (1 + s)




theorem invStereoN_on_sphere (n : ℕ) (x : Fin n → ℝ) :
    ∑ i : Fin (n + 1), (invStereoN n x i) ^ 2 = 1 := by
  unfold invStereoN;
  norm_num [ Finset.sum_add_distrib, Finset.mul_sum _ _ _, mul_pow, Finset.sum_mul _ _ _, div_pow ];
  norm_num [ Finset.sum_ite, Fin.sum_univ_castSucc ];
  norm_num [ ← Finset.mul_sum _ _ _, ← Finset.sum_div ];
  rw [ ← add_div, div_eq_iff ] <;> nlinarith [ show 0 ≤ ∑ i, x i ^ 2 from Finset.sum_nonneg fun _ _ => sq_nonneg _ ]




theorem hypothesis_crystallization (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : ∀ x, f (f x) = f x) (x : ℝ) :
    f (f x) = f x := hf x

-- H4: Idempotent partition into fixed/non-fixed



theorem idem_partition {α : Type*} [DecidableEq α] (f : α → α)
    (hf : ∀ x, f (f x) = f x) (x : α) :
    f x = x ∨ (f x ≠ x ∧ f (f x) = f x) := by
  by_cases h : f x = x
  · exact Or.inl h
  · exact Or.inr ⟨h, hf x⟩




end

# Future Directions: Proof-Theoretic Ordinal Analysis II

This cycle established the structural backbone of the OrdinalTheory framework (file Pythagorean/ProofTheoreticOrdinalsLattice.lean, extending the catalog file Catalog/Pythagorean/ProofTheoreticOrdinals.lean). The main new results are:

- Totality of inclusion (provablyWO_subset_total, le_total_theory): any two OrdinalTheorys are comparable — the space of theories is a chain, not merely a poset. This is sharper than the catalog's observation that pto is not an order embedding.
- pto is a lattice homomorphism (pto_meet_eq_min together with pto_join_eq_max): the proof-theoretic ordinal preserves both meet and join.
- Exact chain additivity of the depth metric (depthDist_chain_additive): along a chain T1 <= T2 <= T3, depthDist T1 T3 = depthDist T1 T2 + depthDist T2 T3 exactly — not merely sub-additively. The directed triangle inequality (depthDist_directed_triangle) is a corollary.
- Failure of the unconditional triangle inequality (depthDist_triangle_general_false): with PTOs omega+1, omega, 0 the inequality breaks, since 1 + omega = omega < omega+1. So depthDist is a genuinely directed quasi-metric.
- PTO fibers are order-convex (pto_constant_on_interval): if the endpoints of an interval share a PTO, the PTO is constant throughout it.

The directions below extend these results.

## 1. Ordinal Notation Systems and the epsilon-0 Barrier
Connect the abstract OrdinalTheory framework to computable ordinal notation systems (Mathlib's ONote and NONote, ordinal notations below epsilon-0). The pto_ofOrdinal_limit theorem establishes that limit ordinals faithfully represent theories for abstract ordinals; linking to ONote would give decidable theory comparison for theories with PTO below epsilon-0. The Iio_sSup_subset_initSeg half-saturation theorem (every ordinal below the PTO is provable) is the structural lemma needed to map between notation-system provability and set-theoretic provability.
Testable conjecture: For every ONote value n, OrdinalTheory.ofOrdinal n.repr has PTO exactly n.repr, and the inclusion ordering on such theories is decidable via the ordering on ONote.

## 2. The Quasi-Metric Geometry of Theory Space
depthDist is symmetric and positive-definite (depthDist_comm, depthDist_self_eq_zero, depthDist_eq_zero_iff). The triangle inequality fails in general due to non-commutativity of ordinal addition, but pto_sandwich suggests a directed triangle inequality holds: ordinal subtraction satisfies (a-b)+(b-c) >= a-c when a >= b >= c. pto_monotone gives the directed structure.
Testable conjecture: For theories T1 <= T2 <= T3, depthDist T1 T3 <= depthDist T1 T2 + depthDist T2 T3, and this fails without the ordering assumption.

## 3. Lattice Structure of OrdinalTheories
join_pto_eq_max shows the join is well-behaved with respect to PTOs. Next: formalize meet (intersection) and show OrdinalTheory forms a complete lattice under inclusion with PTO a lattice homomorphism to the ordinals. Care needed because sSup (S1 cap S2) is not always min(sSup S1, sSup S2). Strict inclusion does NOT imply strict PTO increase (the {b | b < omega} vs {b | b <= omega} counterexample), so the PTO map is not an order embedding; characterizing its fibers is the right structural question.
Testable conjecture: The fibers of the PTO map are intervals in the inclusion lattice: if T1 <= T2 and pto(T1) = pto(T2) = alpha, then for any T with T1 <= T <= T2, pto(T) = alpha.

## 4. Connecting to Concrete Theories via Fast-Growing Hierarchies
Connect the abstract framework to Mathlib's ONote.fastGrowing hierarchy. A theory T knows about ordinal alpha if alpha in T.provablyWO, and f_alpha is a computational witness: T should prove totality of f_alpha for exactly those alpha in its provablyWO set. pto_le_of_not_mem gives the characterization: if alpha not in provablyWO, then alpha >= pto(T), the boundary where the fast-growing hierarchy becomes unprovably total.
Testable conjecture: There exists a computable function from ONote to OrdinalTheory such that the PTO of the resulting theory equals the ordinal represented by the notation, and the theory's provablyWO set coincides with the set of notations whose fast-growing functions are provably total.

## 5. Well-Quasi-Order Structure Under Bounded PTO
pto_monotone shows infinite ascending chains of theories produce infinite ascending sequences of ordinals. Ordinals below a fixed bound are well-ordered, so theories with PTO below alpha admit no infinite strictly ascending chain of PTOs. This gives a well-directed structure: every infinite sequence of theories with bounded PTO has an infinite weakly increasing subsequence in the PTO ordering. The PTO fibers add complexity beyond standard WQO theory.
Testable conjecture: The quotient of {T : OrdinalTheory | T.pto < epsilon-0} by PTO-equivalence (T1 ~ T2 iff pto(T1) = pto(T2)) is a well-order isomorphic to epsilon-0, and each equivalence class is a complete lattice under theory inclusion.

## Companion: extending the EML / oracle infrastructure
- Lift the tight depth hierarchy to the full fragment with controlled inv usage, quantifying exactly how many extra depth levels reciprocals can save.
- Generalize the polynomial-argument majorant to multivariate EML and to other transcendental primitives (log, trigonometric).
- Develop the idempotent-oracle preorder into a verified framework for self-improving numerical solvers, with convergence guarantees from one-step idempotence.
